items_missed: Never got or used the customer's name — she is addressed only as 'ma'am' for the entire 13.9-minute call, and the name is never used once (Section 8 auto-fail).
No 'How are you today?' — jumped straight from the greeting into the qualifying question.
Never confirmed the move date or checked availability on it; the morning window (8:30-9:00 AM) is mentioned in the On-Time Guarantee pitch but the date itself is never verified.
No 'pricing is super simple' opener — went straight to 'I'll jump into the pricing structure.'

Included-items list was framed only as negatives (no fuel/credit card/stair/elevator fees); never named the materials that ARE included — wrap, pads, bands, tape, tools — which matters on a full-pack job where the customer is being charged separately for supplies.
No clock sense-check — never asked 'does that make sense?' after the 2.5-hour minimum / 15-minute increment explanation.
Gave a single-point estimate (6 hours, $1,374) instead of a typical time RANGE for a 900 sq ft one-bedroom full pack.
Elevator and walk distance were probed but never explained as time variables in the estimate, even though both origin (18th floor) and destination (14th floor) are high-rise elevator moves.
No equivalents or reference points (school bus, etc.) used to make the estimate tangible.
Entire Save Your Ass prep speech missing — no 'prep before move day = shorter move = lower bill', no consolidation tips, no 'take a carload' tip, no closing sense-check.

Never mentioned the bolded detail list at the top of the confirmation email or asked her to reply with corrections — a real risk on this call, since he twice read back her origin unit number wrong ('1518' when she said 1818).
Never asked 'any other questions before I let you go?'
Gave contact methods (text/call/email) but no business hours.
No 60 cents/lb baseline valuation mentioned alongside the No Worries coverage.

Never asked the moving-stressor question ('anything you're particularly worried about with this move?') — asked about fragile/antique items instead, which is an inventory question, not a pain-point question.
No rapport moment anywhere in the call — customer answered 'Okay' roughly fifteen consecutive times during the pricing block with no check-in from the rep.
top_strength: The discovery block was genuinely thorough and well-sequenced — he pulled the quote form up front, confirmed both addresses and floors, probed heavy/fragile items, walk distance to the elevator at both ends, loading dock and parking access, extra rooms, extra stops, and then drilled into kitchen density ('is every drawer and cupboard full?') to size the packing job. That specificity is what let him build a defensible 3-hour packing allocation instead of guessing.
coaching_note: When the customer said 'I have a call at three, I need to hop off,' Cameron answered 'I'll make it quicker than that' and then delivered pricing, clock, perks, estimate and scheduling as one uninterrupted ~400-word monologue — she said 'Okay' fifteen times and booked nothing. Speed is not the same as compression. The fix is to cut, not to talk faster: on a time-boxed call, keep the estimate reasoning and the Save Your Ass prep speech (which vanished entirely here and is the section that actually lowers her bill), and drop the detail. And build in a sense-check after the clock explanation — 'does that make sense so far?' — because that is the one moment where a string of 'okay's would have told him whether she was following or just waiting for him to finish.
phone_presence_notes: Polite and professional throughout ('yes ma'am', 'no problem', 'have a wonderful day') and he did acknowledge her 3 PM hard stop, but he never used her name once, never acknowledged any emotion, and the customer stayed monosyllabic for the entire back half of the call.
audio_review_reason: Transcript quality is poor in several stretches (garbled greeting, 'this is cameras moving company', repeated number mis-hears), and the customer is monosyllabic through the whole pricing block — audio is needed to tell whether the flat read is the rep's delivery or an artifact of the transcription.
